Vienna, October 4, 1824.

My dear Marie,

I am sitting down to report to you how the day passed that was granted to me here in Vienna. The trouble of the journey is now settled; my effects have been handed over to the carrier, and I was able to devote myself to the actual life of the city.

I visited the Italian Theatre, where on this day, the feast of Saint Francis, a folk song was performed. The weather was rainy, which prevented the usual illuminations, yet the house was filled to the last seat. The influx was due not only to the feast, but also to the fact that the German Opera was performed for the first time on this day. One saw many beautiful ladies, and because the stage was occupied by Italians, I could concentrate more on the Viennese society gathered there.

The performance of the folk song was remarkable in its simple grandeur. The female side was led by Mrs. Fodor, followed by Dardanelli and others; in total, thirteen women sang. The male side was under the direction of Mr. David, supported by Donzelli, Rubini, Lablache, Ambrogi, Bassi, da Franco, and others; there were sixteen men in total. It was a pure unison song, without solos or variations. The men wore black, the women white satin.

What particularly moved me was the sound. The Italian singers possessed a tone free of longing from the very first moment. Their natural metal was immediately ignited and set in motion. The first tone was freedom and passion; it went with a free chest and soul. The divine fury is by nature melodic. In contrast stood the German Opera, which offered French music by Auber. It was sung by German voices and German women. Only in the last act, when a French coup brought passion into the voices, did it reach a similar intensity.

As for my affairs: The costs incurred by me were charged to the Christians and used for my benefit. I could not ascertain any further festivities. My additions to my effects were classified as travel expenses.

I think of you and the children in Berlin, while here I observe this foreign, yet so lively culture. The movement of freedom shows itself here in art, in the voice, in the way people gather in the hall. It is a different form of freedom than that of our German spirit, yet it is no less genuine in its own form.

Your
Georg

Marie,

I am writing to you from Vienna on October 4th. The day has been full of impressions, and my effects, which I had arranged to be handed over to the freight forwarder, are now secured, with the additions to my luggage classified simply as travel expenses. I have settled my accounts with the Christians here, using the funds for my own needs, though I confess I have heard of no further festivities beyond what I have already experienced.

The weather was rainy, which prevented the illuminations that were likely planned for St. Francis's Day, yet the Italian Theatre was crowded full. The house was packed, partly for the occasion and partly because the German Opera was being performed for the first time that day. I attended an evening of folk songs, a performance that was unison throughout, without any solos or variations. The female side of the ensemble was led by Sra Fodor, and included Dardanelli and others, totaling thirteen singers who wore white satin. The male side was led by Signor David, with Donzelli, Rubini, Lablache, Ambrogi, Bassi, da Franco, and others, totaling sixteen men, all dressed in black.

I must tell you, the difference in the voices was striking. The Italian singers possessed a natural metal that was ignited and in motion from the very first moment. Their sound was free of longing; the first tone went forth with a free breast and soul. It is as if the divine Furore is melodious by nature for them, so that the first sound is already freedom and passion.

In contrast, the German Opera featured French music by Auber, performed by German voices. It was only in the last act, when a French coup was depicted, that passion entered the voices. Until then, the performance lacked that spontaneous fire I found in the Italian ensemble. I saw several pretty ladies in the audience, and because there were no Italians on stage during the opera, I observed the Viennese ladies more closely. It is a pleasure to see the local society engaged in such cultural events, even if the music is French performed by Germans.

I am well and in good spirits. The journey continues, and I hope this letter finds you and the boys in good health. Do not worry about me; I am taking care of my business matters and enjoying the cultural life of this city. I will write again when I can.

Your loving husband,

Hegel

My dear Marie!

I am sitting in Vienna and writing these lines to you while the news of the day is still fresh in my mind. My effects were handed over to the freight carrier today; it is a formal act that transitions the journey into a new section. I have settled my accounts with the Christians and used the money for my own needs, recording my additions to the effects as travel expenses.

The evening was dedicated to the Italian Theatre. It was the day of St. Francis, and the event consisted of a folk song performance. The rainy sky prevented the planned illuminations, which gave the whole thing a rather sober, though no less solemn, character.

The performance itself was unusual. There were no solos, no variations, but a pure unisono. The women were led by Sra Fodor, together with Dardanelli and others, thirteen singers in total. They wore white satin. The men were led by Signor David, with Donzelli, Rubini, Lablache, Ambrogi, Bassi, da Franco and others; sixteen men in black.

What interested me most about the matter was the contrast in sound. The German voices, which had previously appeared in the framework of the German opera – which took place for the first time on this day – sang French music by Auber. Only in the last act, through a French turn, did passion enter these voices. But the Italian singers had a toneless, yearning tone from the first second. Their natural metal was ignited and in motion. The first tone sounded like freedom and passion, with a free chest and soul. The divine Furore is by nature melodic.

The house was fully occupied, partly because of St. Francis, partly because of the premiere of the German opera. Since no Italians were on stage, I could observe more of the Viennese ladies; I saw several beautiful ladies, which is never difficult in this city.

It is a day on which one notices how art shapes the spirit, but also how circumstances – rain, the type of performance – direct perception. I have been able to learn of no further festivities for the coming days.

Farewell and greet the children.

Your
Georg

My dear Marie,

It has grown late; I am only now, around eleven o'clock, coming home and must tell you what happened today in Vienna. Yesterday morning I visited several churches and subsequently examined the collections of Archduke Charles. I was particularly fascinated by the drawings and prints in the portfolios; the collection comprises no less than 150,000 prints. I spent a long time with the sheets by Michelangelo and also viewed the procession by Mantegna, which was shown to me by Privy Councillor Schultz. I also studied the portfolios by Martin Schongauer and other artists. The director stayed with me for almost three hours to discuss these works.

In the evening there was the performance; the ballets were excellent, with superb leaps, though without the usual leg extensions. The audience had hardly any time to laugh, as constantly new and varied things appeared on stage. It was more entertaining than the first drama. I hope you and the boys are well.

Yours
G. W. F. Hegel

Marie,

I arrived here only shortly before eleven, but the day was so full that fatigue hardly affects me. Yesterday morning I looked around in several churches, but this morning the true treasure was in the house of the Privy Councillor Schultz. There I had the opportunity to study the drawings and prints of Archduke Charles. The director was so kind as to stay with me for almost three hours while we went through the portfolios. They speak of 150,000 prints! I worked particularly through the sheets by Michelangelo and viewed Mantegna’s procession. Martin Schongauer and other masters were also represented therein.

In the evening I was again at the theater. The ballet was excellent, the jumps were superb. There were no leg positions, but the audience had hardly time to laugh, as constantly new and different things appeared. It was more entertaining than the first tragedy. I am healthy and cheerful, but I look forward to being with you again soon. Kiss the children from me.

Your G. W. F. Hegel

Vienna, Saturday, Sept. 25.

Dear Marie,

It is almost eleven o’clock since I came home. The day was rich in experiences that do not quite let me rest. Yesterday morning I visited several churches, but today my time was devoted to drawing and etching. The Director stayed with me for almost three hours to show me the collection of Archduke Charles. There are 150,000 etchings in portfolios; we went through the sheets by Michelangelo, then Mantegna’s procession – which can also be seen at Councillor of State Schultz’s – as well as Martin Schongauer and some other masters.

In the evening there was the performance, which proved more entertaining than the first drama. The dance pieces were excellent in their leaps, although no leg extensions occurred. The audience had hardly time to laugh, as constantly new and different things appeared. I am tired, but satisfied. Kiss the children from me.

Your faithful H.

Vienna, October 2nd, Saturday evening.

My dear Marie,

This morning I went to the Esterházy collection for the third time. The finest pieces are located in the Prince's private room, a garden room in the pavilion next to the large painting gallery. The Prince himself was in the room and asked who was there when he heard me walking around. It was not a public day, but when he learned that the visitor was a professor from Berlin who was coming for the third time, he ordered the chamberlain to show me everything. Shortly thereafter, he left the room. I saw the pieces of the cabinet once more. One must imagine this: This Prince can travel several miles from Vienna on his own land up to the Turkish border. I was there from nine to eleven o'clock. The journey home took half an hour.

After I had changed my clothes, I went to the antiquities cabinet. The director, Professor Sonnleitner, had invited me. He is unmarried. We dined with him and a professor from Padua in an inn. The man from Padua is very learned and amiable. In the afternoon, I took some walks in the city.

In the evening, I was at the Italian Opera. They performed *Corradino il cuor di ferro*. Dardanelli sang, and David sang with Dardanelli. It was a pleasant evening. Last evening, I spoke at dinner with a man who claimed that Rossini's music is music for the heart. I do not know if one may say so, but it was a friendly evening.

The city has its charms, but I miss the quiet order of our home. I often think of you and the children. The heat is still there, but the evenings are becoming cooler. I hope you are all well. I will return soon. Until then, I greet you warmly.

Your
G. W. F. Hegel

Vienna, October 2nd, Saturday Evening.

My dear Marie,

I am writing to you today about a day that gave me great pleasure, because I was once again among the things I love. In the morning, I was for the third time in the Esterházy Collection. The very best pieces are located in the Prince's private room, a garden room in the pavilion next to the castle, where the large gallery is. The Prince himself was just there and asked who was present when he heard me moving. It was not a public day, but he learned that the visitor was a professor from Berlin who was here for the third time. Thereupon, he ordered the chamberlain to show me everything. The Prince left shortly after, and I was able to examine the pieces of the cabinet once more in peace. One must imagine: This Prince can drive several miles on his own land from Vienna, right up to the Turkish border. I was there from nine to eleven o'clock, and the half hour I walked home did me good.

After I had changed, I went to the Antiquities Cabinet. There I was invited by the director, Professor Sonnleitner, who is unmarried. We dined there with a professor from Padua, a very learned and amiable man. After the meal, I took some walks in the city and spent the evening at the Italian Opera. They performed *Corradino il cuor di ferro*. Dardanelli sang, and David sang with him. That was a true delight.

Last evening at dinner, I spoke with a man who claimed that Rossini's music is music for the heart. I have thought about this while I was looking at the old masters today. There is a difference between what immediately moves the heart and what addresses the mind in its entire sublimity. But I do not wish to burden you with my thoughts. I am glad that I am here and can enjoy this quiet and this art. Think of me, and send your warm regards to the children.

Your faithful husband

My dear Marie,

The paid servant brought me your letter today. It arrived safely, and the man received me very kindly. The happy news contained in it of your well-being touched me deeply. I am now in Prague, which brings me half the distance closer to you. Here I enjoy intellectual pleasures and literally live in utopias. I have seen and heard so much beautiful that I lack the words to describe it to you completely.

It was often a tormenting worry to me that I so much surrender myself to this beauty and these utopias, while I asked myself how it was going with you. Your well-being is the only condition under which my own happiness and my intellectual refreshment are not accompanied by a bad conscience. You have had to forgo many of the pleasures that I was allowed to enjoy alone, without you. I wish I could bring back all the beautiful things I have experienced. But please, be content with me as the main good. Imagine how you would answer this question – I am sure it would be with the same intimacy that fills me here.

Your
G. W. F. H.

My dear Marie,

The paid servant brought me your letter today, which arrived perfectly intact, and I accept it gladly. The news of your well-being was the long-awaited pleasant message that means so much to me. I am now in Prague and have thereby come half the distance closer to you.

Confess it: I am enjoying intellectual pleasures here and living, as it were, in utopias. I have seen and heard so much that is beautiful. Yet often the disturbing thought tormented me that I am enjoying so much beauty here and living in such dreams, while I wondered whether you are well. Had I not received your news, I would have had a bad conscience regarding my own well-being. So many pleasures have been lacking to you, which I alone enjoyed without you at my side.

I wish I could bring all the beauty I have seen and heard to you. But I ask you, be satisfied with me as the main thing. Imagine how you would answer this question – with that quiet understanding that only we share.

Your
G. W. F. H.

My dear Marie,

The paid servant brought my letter today, which, as he assured me, was delivered correctly, and I received from him the news I so urgently needed: You are well. I am sitting here in Prague and am now already half as close to you as I should be.

I confess to you openly: I have indulged in mental pleasures and live almost in utopias. I have seen and heard so much beauty that my conscience was heavy as long as I did not know how you were faring. The troubling thought often came to me that I am here basking in this abundance of beauty, while I wondered if you were well. You have deprived me of so many pleasures that I have enjoyed alone, and I wish I could bring all the beautiful things I have experienced back home.

But I beg you, be content with me as the main thing. Imagine how you would answer this question!

Your faithful husband

My dear Marie,

I returned to Vienna early this morning, having been in the Prater yesterday afternoon. It resembles our Tiergarten, but is laid out with broader avenues and the ground is more green. There are several large open green spaces. Countless small taverns are scattered throughout, entirely in the style of Moabit or Pankow, nothing like our tents or gardeners. One must have seen the Prater to truly get to know Vienna. The heat is still there, but the air is fresh. I often think of you and the children. Good night.

Your G.W.F. Hegel

Marie,

On Saturday afternoon we went for a walk in the Prater. It resembles our Zoo, but is covered with more grass and has much larger open spaces. The avenues are wider and trimmed. Everywhere stand countless taverns, entirely in the style of Moabit or Pankow, nothing like our tents or gardens. One must have been there to truly see Vienna. It was a pleasant walk, and I often think of you.

Your G. W. F. Hegel

My dear Marie,

Yesterday afternoon I was in the Prater. It is a forest like our Tiergarten, but the avenues are wider and the ground is more densely covered with grass. There are several larger open green spaces. Everywhere countless stalls are set up, which do not resemble our tents or court gardeners, but rather have the style of Moabit or Pankow. One must have seen the Prater to have truly gotten to know Vienna. I am well and will continue my journey tomorrow.

Your
G. W. F. Hegel

Prague, September 17, 1824

My dear Marie,

Yesterday I spent the whole day traveling to Karlštejn, an old fortress located four hours away. There hang old paintings that can be viewed. This morning I visited the churches and galleries, partly by repeating previous visits, until I had seen all the sights. The heat of yesterday and this morning has greatly weakened and sensitized me. For lunch today I was at Uncle’s house. There I felt very well. After the meal, he drove with me in a carriage to a pleasant place of amusement. It has not rained for a long time, and the leaves are still firm and green. Tomorrow I will dine at the same house.

Your faithful G. W. F. Hegel

Prague, Friday evening, Sept. 17.

My dear, yesterday I spent the whole day on a tour to Karlštejn, four hours from here. It is an old castle in which old paintings hang. This morning I visited churches and galleries, partly repeating earlier visits to complete the sights. The heat of yesterday and today has greatly weakened and exhausted me. For lunch I was at Uncle’s, where I felt very well. After the meal he drove with me in a carriage to a pleasant place of amusement. It has not rained for a long time, and the leaves are still firm and green. I shall dine with him again tomorrow. As you see, I am well taken care of here, even though my body suffers from the heat.

Your
Hegel

Prague, September 17, Evening.

Yesterday I spent the whole day on the journey to Karlštejn, which takes four hours. The old castle is worth seeing; old paintings hang in it. This morning I visited churches and galleries, partly repeating earlier visits; now I have seen the city, what I wanted to see. But the heat of yesterday and this morning has greatly weakened and affected me. I had lunch at my uncle's; after the meal he drove with me in a carriage to a pleasant place of recreation. It has not rained for a long time, the leaves are still firm and green. I found myself very well at my uncle's. Tomorrow I dine there again. The days pass quietly, and I am glad to have the main occupations of the trip behind me, even if my body still lags somewhat.

Your
G. W. F.

Vienna, September 28.

Dear Marie,

I am writing to you from the inner part of Vienna; I have not yet come closer to the outer suburbs. My street, the Kärntner, reminds me strongly of our Königsstraße, but here the straight lines are entirely lacking. The lanes are narrow, flanked by immense palaces, but I miss the architectural beauty that I appreciate on the Linden or the Leipziger Straße. The Castle itself stands there, in the style of the Dresden Residence, and one almost asks oneself where its true facade is hidden. A new gate has only been there for a year, and a Temple of Theseus, which reminds one of our Hauptwache, also stands in the area.

Today I went immediately to the Volksgarten, at the urging of Madame Milder. Between the city and the suburb, the paths are green and fresh, still without the autumnal shimmer that we know in Berlin. I have not yet visited the Prater and the Augarten; the art transactions must first be completed.

Your
G. W. F. Hegel

Vienna, September 28.

Dear Marie,

I am writing to you briefly, as the day is still fresh in my memory. I have not yet reached outer Vienna, but have stayed exclusively in the Inner City, the actual city without the suburbs. My street is the Kärntner, which involuntarily reminds me of the Königsstraße. There are hardly any straight streets here; instead, enormous palaces and narrow lanes define the scene. I miss the width and the architectural beauty of the Linden, the Leipziger, or the Wilhelmsstraße. The Castle itself is in the style of the Dresden Palace, one finds hardly a clear facade, and a new gate has existed for only one year. There is also a Temple of Theseus, which reminds me of our Hauptwache.

On the order of Mlle. Milder, I immediately went to the Volksgarten, where Lilli accompanied me. The walking paths between the city and the suburbs are pleasant, green, and fresh, not yet autumnal like here in Berlin. I have not yet visited the Prater and the Augarten, as I must first conclude my business affairs in the art trade.

Your G. W. F. Hegel

My dear!

I am here in the Inner City, on the Kärntner Straße. The area is magnificent in its layout, yet the streets are narrow and there is hardly a straight line. I compared the possible through-views with our linden trees, the Leipziger and the Wilhelmsstraße, but I rarely find architecturally beautiful buildings here. The palaces are enormous, yet the castle itself strikes me as the palace in Dresden; one hardly knows where the facade actually is, and the new gate has already existed for a year. The Temple of Theseus in the style of the Hauptwache also caught my eye.

Today I went with Lilli to the Volksgarten, on the orders of Madame Milder. Between the city and the suburbs there are pleasant, green and fresh walking paths, which are not yet autumnal, as we know it in Berlin. I have not yet visited the Prater and the Augarten, for the art transactions must first be settled.

Give the children my kisses.

Your
G. W. F. Hegel

My dear Marie,

I was yesterday in the Imperial and Royal Library and admired the engravings, a collection numbering a hundred thousand copies; it would take three years to go through them daily at three hundred sheets. In the afternoon I visited the Belvedere and then went with Mr. Ruß to the observatory.

In the evening I sat in the Italian Theatre and heard Rossini's *Barber of Seville* for the second time. The singers performed the piece with true love, but my taste is now spoiled: Rossini's Figaro pleases me infinitely better than Mozart's *Marriage*. I can hardly leave Vienna.

Your faithful husband

G. W. F. Hegel

Dear Marie,

Yesterday morning we took a walk and visited the Imperial and Royal Library, where I saw a scholarly collection of engravings. Your Georg

My dear Marie,

Yesterday morning I visited the Imperial and Royal Library and saw there a scholarly collection of 300,000 engraving plates. Archduke Charles's collection is a different one. It would take three years to see it at a rate of 300 sheets per day. In the afternoon I was at the Belvedere and went with Mr. Ruß to the observatory. Your faithful
Hegel

Vienna, September 25.

Dear Marie,

I am writing to you about my walk through the capital today. The day began with a visit to the imperial private gardens and the greenhouses of the Castle. One enters and exits there through a kind of underground passage; the Emperor himself uses this passage daily and spends his afternoons in his gardens. I had expected more from the flora there, hoping for magnificent georginas and althea, but the flowers were, frankly, rather insignificant. The situation on the Peacock Island is probably quite different, as I was told.

I spent the afternoon at the Belvedere, where I lingered for a few more hours to prepare for the main event of the evening: Rossini’s “Barber of Seville.” We attended the performance, and I must confess to you that the evening was a triumph, even though the music bored me somewhat in places. The cast is phenomenal. Lablache sang Figaro; he is a bass who appears cheerful and freely comic, without ever showing anything cute or vulgar in his portrayal. His talent is so natural that even when the entire choir sings and the orchestra enters with full force in fortissimo, he seems to sound like a soloist. He sings this without strain, without shouting, and without that screaming tone one often hears.

Mme Fodor as Rosine is a perfect singer. She unites beauty, grace, art, freedom, and taste in her singing. Ambrogi played Doctor Bartolo very well, and a new singer, de Franco, also contributed. The entire company consists of a whole series of the most excellent and flawless singers.

The audience participates actively. Three to four performers are applauded at their first appearance, and every passage is greeted with “Bravo! Bravi!” After each scene, the applause rages excessively. The singer thanks the audience and leaves the stage, but the clapping continues with such constant strength that the singer is not only applauded but actually “applauded out.” At the end of the piece, there are no shouts or speeches.

The theater press in Vienna reports that the most experienced critics are of the opinion that in 50 years—as far as their memory reaches—there has been no such Italian company in Vienna. It is certain that in the next 50 years no such company will come again. The party guests, whom I had persuaded not to miss the performance, were collectively highly delighted, although they disparaged Rossini’s music. One cannot experience the “Barber of Seville” anywhere else in Italy with such festivity and other things as here.

Your
G. W. F. Hegel

Vienna, 25 September 1824

My dear Marie,

I am now sitting at my desk in the evening to report to you how today has passed in this great city. In the morning I visited the Imperial Private Garden and the greenhouses in the palace. One goes in and out through a kind of underground passage; the Emperor himself traverses this path daily. He spends some afternoon hours in his gardens, yet my expectations regarding the flora were rather modest. I had hoped for geraniums and altheas, but the flowers I saw there were quite insignificant. The situation on the Peacock Island is, however, quite different; it must be far more magnificent there. I spent the afternoon at the Belvedere, where I was able to collect myself in the quiet, before I escaped to the noise of the opera.

In the evening I was at Rossini's *Figaro*. Lablache sang Figaro, and Mde Fodor Rosine. Mde Fodor is a perfect singer; she possesses beauty, grace, art, freedom, and taste in her singing. Lablache, a bass, is cheerful and freely comic; in his portrayal there is nothing dainty or vulgar. It is astonishing that, when the whole chorus sings and the orchestra crashes in at fortissimo with all its might, it sounds as if Lablache were singing solos. He accomplishes this without effort, without shouting, and without a single shouting tone. Ambrogi played Doctor Bartolo very well, and a new singer, de Franco, was also on stage. The entire company consists of a whole fence of the most distinguished and flawless singers.

The audience takes lively part in the performance. Three to four actors are applauded at their first appearance. Every passage is applauded or called out with “bravo! bravi!” After each scene the audience applauds boundlessly. The singer thanks them and goes off, yet the clapping continues with sustained force, so that the singer is not merely applauded, but properly “applauded out.” At the end of the piece there is no calling out or speaking. One cannot enjoy *Figaro* anywhere else in Italy with so much partisanship and others. I read today in a Viennese theater sheet that the most experienced are of the opinion that, in the last 50 years, as far as their memory reaches, no such Italian company has been in Vienna. It is certain that such a company will not come again in the next 50 years.

The Parteyshens, whom I first had to persuade, have not missed a performance. They were collectively the most enthusiastic, although they disparaged Rossini's music. I confess that Rossini's music sometimes bores me as music, but the performance here is of a quality that has no equal.

Your
Hegel

Vienna, September 25.

My dear Marie,

The day has kept me busy in many ways, but I am well. In the morning I visited the Imperial Private Garden and the greenhouses at the Palace. One gets there through a peculiar underground passage, which the Emperor himself walks through every day. He spends some afternoon hours there. I had been looking forward to the georines and altheas, but the flowers were rather insignificant. The situation is quite different on the Peacock Island, where nature can unfold more freely.

In the afternoon I spent some hours at the Belvedere, and then in the evening I attended the performance of Rossini's *Figaro*. The performance was a true festival. Lablache sang Figaro, and Mme Fodor sang Rosine. The latter is a perfect singer; she combines beauty, grace, art, freedom, and taste in her singing in an admirable way. Lablache, a bass, is cheerful and freely comic; there is nothing low or vulgar in his performance. When the whole chorus sings and the orchestra enters with full force fortissimo, it sounds as if Lablache were singing alone. He sings this without strain, without shouting, and without a single shouting tone. Ambrogi as Dr. Bartolo was also very good, and a new singer, de Franco, also appeared. The company consists of a whole hedge of the most excellent and model singers.

The audience takes lively part in the play. Three to four performers are applauded at their first appearance. Every passage is applauded or greeted with "bravo! bravi!" After each scene the audience applauds excessively. The singer thanks the audience and leaves, but the applause continues with sustained strength, so that the singer is not merely applauded but properly "beaten" with applause. At the end of the piece there is no calling out or speaking. One cannot see the *Figaro* anywhere else in Italy with such jubilation and such an audience. I read today in a Viennese theater sheet that the most experienced people are of the opinion that, according to their longest memory, no such Italian company has been in Vienna for 50 years. It is certain that no such company will return in the next 50 years.

The party guests, whom I first had to persuade not to miss a performance, were collectively most delighted. However, they despised the music of Rossini. The music of Rossini sometimes bores me as music, but the performance was unsurpassed. The Viennese theater sheets agree in this opinion.

Kiss the children from me affectionately.

Your faithful husband and father

Hegel

My dear Marie,

I am writing to you from Vienna, where the sky cleared up again this afternoon. Yesterday, the first scene of the ballet was performed for the last time. The German Eberle danced excellently, but he lacked that Italian style one admires in a Torelli. The latter had a superior manner and a Roman physiognomy that struck me.

I went this morning to the Imperial and Royal Library. There one sees daily, on certain days, the treasures of artistic genius – Raphael and Marcantonio – and that for free. One gives a tip to the serving staff. I have always done this, even when it was not necessary. In Vienna, however, I gave these gifts to do honor to the royal Prussian professional dignity. For here, as in the whole world, the “Berlin-Potsdam dirtiness” is notorious. One reads in the local newspapers how highly the “Prophet Dittmar” is esteemed, that Berliner who predicts the weather. His homeland, however, is not here. I myself am, after all, a public ordinary professor of philosophy at the Royal University in Berlin.

My journey did not take me through Swabia, but via Nuremberg to Berlin. It is a strange feeling to be here in Vienna, where one is viewed with a certain distrust as a Berliner. The people here appreciate the order and splendor that we cultivate in Prussia, yet they know the harshness that accompanies our discipline. I often think of our sons Karl and Immanuel, and of Ludwig. In the library, surrounded by the silence of art, I feel the distance from our home.

The art here is great, but it is also a mirror of society. As in the history of freedom, so also in aesthetics: The individual must be sublated in the universal to become true. Eberle’s dance was good, but Torelli’s posture carried the weight of antiquity within it. It is a lesson that also applies to us: We must submit to discipline in order to attain freedom.

I hope that Karl and Immanuel are getting along well at school and show the necessary calm and attention. The school must mediate between the love of the family and the world of action. I expect that they learn to follow before they judge.

Stay healthy, my dear Marie. I am drinking a good wine here and thinking of you.

Your
G. W. F. Hegel

My dear Marie,

I have always done this, even if it was not strictly necessary, to preserve the honor of my office and the Prussian professorship. One must know that the so-called "Berlin-Potsdam dirtiness" is notorious here and throughout the world; I therefore wanted to counter the bad reputation of my homeland through my politeness and show that philosophy and decorum are inseparable.

Yesterday was the last performance of the first act of the ballet. Eberle, a German, danced excellently, although he lacked the Italian turn of a Torelli. However, Torelli possessed an admirable manner and a Roman physiognomy that immediately caught my eye. It is fascinating how national character manifests in the physical, as in the mental. Art, like history, is the expression of the spirit in freedom, and even in dance the difference between the German and the Italian nature is reflected.

I think of you and the children. The hardships of the journey are rewarded by such moments of cultural depth. Farewell and greet your family.

Your faithful husband,
G. W. F. Hegel

My dear Marie,

I stood before the works of Raphael and Marc Anton. The presence of these masterpieces in a public space, where one only needs to give a small tip to the attendants, is impressive. I have always tipped generously, even where it was not strictly necessary, for I wanted thereby to maintain the honour of my office. For never forget: I am a royal professor publ. ordin. at the royal university in Berlin, in Philosophy.

Here in Vienna – and in the whole world – our “Berlin-Potsdam dirtiness” is notorious. One sees it everywhere, in the clothing, in the bearing. Perhaps it is good that I am here, to throw my clean, Prussian scholarship into the scales.

One must, however, be honest: He lacked the Italian *Tournure* of a Torelli. The latter, on the other hand, possessed an admirable manner and a true Roman physiognomy. It was a pleasure to see the classical bearing, which distinguishes itself from mere technical skill.

I hope it is well with you and the boys. The absence of Swabia and Nuremberg, which I passed on the way here, took me directly back to Berlin, before I continued on to Vienna. I greet you warmly and think of you, while I enjoy the silence of evening Vienna.

Your
G.W.F. Hegel

Vienna, October 2nd, Sunday Evening.

My dear Marie,

I am writing to you from the inn, where the air here hangs heavier than in Berlin, but the evenings invite reflection. Yesterday I was in the Ambras Collection, where the works of art affected me like silent witnesses of past powers. Then I went to Belvedere and looked for Ruß, who lives nearby. He himself was not there, but his wife and daughter showed me fine engravings by Dürer and other masters. Later we were able to take a walk, which did me good.

In the evening I visited the Theater an der Wien, a house I had not yet seen. It is the most beautiful theater building in the city, I believe. The architecture is imposing, with five tiers, the so-called boxes, and no ground-floor boxes. The house seemed very empty, however, due to its immense height. They performed two plays with the same content. In the second performance, King Frederick II was depicted as a Duke. Prussian names and uniforms were used, based on a well-known anecdote. The Duke was portrayed as humble, old, with a cane and snuff from the breast pocket. A Prussian officer sat next to me, and it was amusing to observe how he referred every gesture of the "Duke" to his own person or at least followed it attentively.

I often think of Karl and Immanuel. World history is the progress in the consciousness of freedom, and even in such local artifices one sees how the idea of freedom and status changes. The Prussian strictness, which is caricatured here on stage, is also part of the ethical life that we cultivate in Germany. I hope you are well. Take care of yourselves.

Your faithful G.W.F. Hegel

My dear Marie,

I am writing to you from Vienna, where the day has passed in a kind of busy leisure. The building is very remarkable in its construction; it has five floors, which are called Stöcke here, and no ground-floor boxes. Two plays of the same content were performed, in which a king incognito enters a family of low standing. In the second play, the figure of Frederick II., here designated as a Duke, appeared with Prussian names and uniforms. Beside me sat a Prussian officer, who followed everything that was said about the Duke with great attention.

The house itself appeared to me very empty, which is probably due to the infinite height of the space, which separates the spectators far from one another. Despite the emptiness and the size, it is the most beautiful theater building in the city, as I find it. Thus I close these lines with the wish that you are all well in Berlin.

Your
Hegel

Vienna, September 25, Evening

Dearest Marie,

I am writing to you again today from my side of the table, for the rest of the day was a single rush. I stand or sit, but my legs carry me through the city, while the spirit rests. It is a kind of fatigue that arises only from walking, not from thinking.

Last evening I was at the Leopoldstadt Theatre, that famous Casperl, of which so much is spoken, but which is often enough mere noise. They do not perform Italian opera there, but a pantomimic ballet. The main figure is a Mr. Ignaz Schuster. He is a small, stooped man, no coarse, low comedian like the Carl I saw in Munich – this Schuster has a certain force, comparable to a Gern or a Köster. His pieces, “the false Prima Donna” and “the Hats in the Theatre,” are neither exceptional nor deeply comic. I saw “the wicked Liesel.” The piece was sentimental and morally lame work. The other actresses and actors were stiff and boring, infinitely stiffer than the mediocre ones in Berlin. It lasted only an hour.

After that followed a pantomime with music. It was the story of Harlequin with his Colombina, which I saw in all details. It consisted of a whole series of comic absurdities, street singing, dance music and noise. Three hours and thirty minutes without interruption! It is a sight that tires the mind, more through the monotony of the roaring than through the content.

This morning I was in the zoological collection. It is rich and very beautifully arranged. The keepers are all extraordinarily obliging, honest and knowledgeable people. Since they are in connection with professors in Berlin, I was received like a colleague. It was a pleasant interruption.

In the afternoon I was persuaded to take part in a maneuver. The Emperor and the entire family were present. Outside, an immense crowd gathered. The Emperor ended the exercise early. I walked for several hours in the meantime. One must not come too close to the Emperor, but the distance was great enough to observe the order.

So I have been on my feet all day, walking, standing or sitting. I sit only now, while I write to you, and in the evening at the theatre. I report further, as I faithfully do.

Your
Hegel

Vienna, September 25.

My dear Marie,

Herzberg, 8 October 1824

Dearest Marie,

The journey so far has been ordinary and bearable, for the weather has turned for the better. On Sunday the sky was overcast, and it rained several times, until we reached Jüterbog. Today, on Monday, I arrived in Herzberg after lunch.

Here I have experienced something unplanned. I asked a rural pastor to arrange a niece as a companion for me to Dresden. The lady was not ugly, but she has grown a little old and possesses a Saxon politeness that did not much encourage me to speak. So the journey was similar to a solitude. A cat-in-the-bag purchase has been made, and the find was not bad, but insignificant.

Immediately upon arrival I went to the inn, where I heard that Privy Councillor Schulze is staying here. I entered the Blue Star and sought him out. He had already prepared everything for a departure today, yet I was able to persuade him to stay with me today. We were both very glad to see each other again.

This morning we first visited Böttiger, then the picture gallery. Afterwards we listened to Böttiger’s lecture, in which we went through the antiquities again. If I were a true English traveller, I would not have declined the company; but I am still deeply German and could not resist the invitation. The encounter was pleasant, and the conversation flowed easily.

I think of you and the boys in Berlin. The silence here is different, but the acquaintance with Schulze makes the days less lonely.

Your faithful
G. W. F. Hegel

Vienna, 28 September 1824, morning

My dear little wife,

I am now sitting in Vienna again and writing to you about my impressions, which here consist mainly of three chapters: the Imperial and Royal Picture Gallery, the Italian opera, and occasional glances at outer Vienna.

I was in the Gallery the morning before yesterday, all day yesterday, and again today. One sees wonderful things there that elevate the spirit and stimulate thought. But my heart belongs here more to music. On Monday Mercadante's *Doralice* was performed. On Tuesday it was Rossini's *Othello* and yesterday Rossini's *Zelmira*.

The singers and singeresses possess a perfection, a power, purity and training that reminds one of Catalani and Mde Milder. Mde Fodor was on stage on Tuesday. Her voice is beautiful, even if it no longer possesses quite that full power as before; yet one may regard this as a conscious, tasteful artistic choice that lends depth to the whole.

My favorite tenor Rubini sang every evening, as did the handsome baritone Donzelli. Both had as much to sing as Bader in *Olympia*. But the tenor David was yesterday and the day before yesterday the most admired and applauded singer. He has a wonderful voice, power and strength. His high notes are indeed falsetto, but light and in a single transition. Also the fine bass Lablache as well as the two handsome basses Botticelli and Cintimarra sang, and yesterday Sgra Dardanelli was heard.

I must confess to you that the sound of all voices in Berlin, with the exception of Milder, compared to the metal of the male voices here in Vienna sounds impure, rough, hard or weak. The male voices here sound like fiery wine, while ours taste like beer. The audience was bored with *Zelmira*, especially in the first part, but that changes nothing regarding the quality of the art.

Kiss the children, especially Karl and Immanuel.

Your
G. W. F. Hegel

Prague, September 11, 1824.

My dear little wife,

I am writing to you from Prague, where I arrived today at eleven o'clock. The day of travel itself was a succession of impressions that I wish to convey to you, as they complete the picture of this region. In Töplitz, I drank from the spring on Sunday and visited the beautiful Clary Park. A bath did me good, and the Schlackenberg offered a worthy view.

At about eleven o'clock, I boarded the carriage and am traveling over the second of the aforementioned mountain ranges. The landscape was fertile, rich, and varied; I saw hills full of fields, meadow valleys, villages, and fruit trees. In half an hour, we crossed the mountains. The further road led downhill or level, apart from small elevations, toward Prague.

From the height of the mountain, an endless view opened to me as far as Lowositz. The landscape was again rich and diverse. Then we drove through flat land, through boring orchards, and crossed the Eger twice. The second time, the moonlight reflections on the water were the most beautiful I have ever seen. We drove to Meldros. The land today was boring, but the valley of the Moldau and the view of Prague from above were pleasant and enveloped in a fragrance.

I have received a letter from you and will act according to your instructions. Uncle Herr is an interesting point that I will take note of.

Your faithful G.W.F.

My dear Marie,

I am sitting in the new inn here in Töplitz, which hangs splendidly on the “King of Prussia.” The road from here led via Abersau to Culm, that place which is famous for the battle of 1807. Immediately after arriving, I climbed the slag hill opposite the house, on the advice of Miss Stok. Then I visited the park of the castle of Prince Clary, the lord of this region, and took a bath in the stone bath, whose spring is wonderful. I ate with a good appetite. The people here are orderly and seem to wish for nothing better than to be in good agreement with one. Tomorrow I will ride to the castle hill. Until then, I remain your faithful Hg.

My dear Marie,

It is Sunday noon, and I am sitting here to tell you about Vienna before I set off on the rest of my journey. This will be my last letter from this city. I went for a walk on the water promenade, but there I only saw middle-class people. The high society does not show itself here on foot, but only in their carriages in the Prater. I saw quite a bit at the opera, but I found nothing special that I could report to you.

What strikes me more is the difference from Berlin. Here, the broad, splashing shoe-and-gaiter business is much more frequent. The city is full of trim shops. The shops are often strangely mixed: meat and sausage shops stand right next to ladies' hats, and silver shops next to rope makers. And what particularly strikes me: schnapps boutiques, schnapps tables, and schnapps taverns are seen everywhere here, whereas one hardly notices them in Berlin.

This evening the first act of *Zelmire-Dardanelli* will be performed. Tomorrow is Franz's Day, and in all the theaters the song "God preserve our good Emperor Franz" will be sung. I had hoped to be able to tell you about the elegance of the ladies, but reality was less impressive.

I wish I could fly faster than the letters, to soon stand before you again.

Your G.W.F. Hegel

Vienna, September 21, 1824

My dear Marie,

I am finally sitting down, after a day that has returned to me the full hardship of travel in its tangible harshness. We left Prague only on Saturday afternoon, and so our flight from slowness began with a departure at six o’clock in the morning. The coachmen of the express carriage had tripled their prices, which gave me little pleasure, yet the comfort was different from usual: the main vehicle was divided by a window-like partition into two cabins, each of which offered space for four persons.

My three traveling companions were a distinguished company. A gentleman and his wife, who were returning from Carlsbad, shared the space with me and a man who had been the personal physician to Archduke Charles for twenty-four years. This gentleman had recently retired to an independent position, which gave him a certain composure that was useful to me in long conversation. In thirty-six hours we covered twenty-four miles, over mountains and through valleys, by day and by night.

The landscape of Bohemia was uniform and fertile farmland. We drove through a part of Moravia, past Collin, Czaslau, Iglau, and Znaim, until we entered proper Austria. Here the picture changed: vineyards, fields, hills, forests, and villages presented themselves in wide views over these rich regions. At the penultimate post station we came near the Danube, without, however, seeing it. The terrain was a deep plain that extended for half a day in monotonous uniformity, without our being able to catch sight of Vienna.

After six o’clock we reached the city. We paid the toll and the post fees, and I hired a fiaker to find a room. At the house “To Archduke Charles” there were no rooms facing the street available, so I took one that opened onto the courtyard, one flight of stairs up. I inquired after Mr. D. Parthey; the young married couple Klein, who were lodging here, had just departed. I accepted the porter’s trunk, as my trunk was still at the customs house.

At seven o’clock I was at the hotel. At half past eight I hurried to the Italian Opera, as Madame Milder had commanded. Mercadante was performed, yet Madame Fodor did not appear in the piece. One heard male voices that filled the scene.

I am still in the dust cloud of travel, and my mind needs rest to order these impressions. I shall have to mention Madame Milder again later, as her influence on my travel planning is not to be underestimated.

Your faithful husband

G. W. F. Hegel

Prague, September 14.

My dear Marie,

I must confess to you that I find this stay in Prague a bit too long; two days, or at least one, are too many for me here. But what is to be done? Yesterday I learned that only one place was left on the express mail to Vienna. So I had to break off everything early in the morning and secure this place. With that, I am bound for Sunday morning and must endure the whole week here.

Today had its charm. I went to the bridge and to the Hradčany. The view there is beautiful, yes, truly very beautiful. I properly looked at the area today. In the famous cathedral I saw old German paintings, but I am not sufficiently knowledgeable to report more to you about them. I also visited the so-called Court Gallery, a collection of private treasures that are united in a magnificent location. There are beautiful and very beautiful pieces among them, especially a collection of old German painting.

After dinner I took a fiacre to the maneuver. When I arrived, the actual maneuver was already over. I therefore stood at the gate and observed how the regiments, especially that of Kutschera, marched out. Suddenly I spotted my uncle at the head of his regiment. He commanded in a stately manner, surrounded by his adjutant, majors, and officers. He noticed me, tore off his cap – as did the others present – and rode to me with a quick movement. He bent from the horse and embraced me warmly. I was forced to decline his invitation to visit him tomorrow, as I had already firmly booked my place on the mail.

It was a touching moment to see this old gentleman in his military dignity, but the schedule left no choice. I hope you forgive me that I must remain here this week.

Your faithful
G. W. F. Hegel

My dear Marie,

I am sitting in Vienna and writing to you about a day that took shape from a series of impressions that are trying to arrange themselves into a whole in my head.

The city itself is enclosed by high ramparts and bastions. One might think this is mere defense, but here they serve as promenades. From these heights one looks down onto the glacis, that wide, flat plain that spreads out before the fortress walls. It is covered with green meadows and intersected by avenues and is excellent for the boys to fly their kites. Beyond this greenery lie the suburbs, a colorful mixture of palaces, gardens, churches, and smaller buildings. As for the Danube, I must confess that it contributes little to the external impression of beauty of the city. Outside the walls, however, a rural, village life prevails, which forms a gentle transition to the open landscape.

My Tuesday was characterized by cultural obligations. In the morning I was in the Esterházy Collection. Around noon I went to Schönbrunn. There I saw neither the menagerie nor the botanical garden, although I was assured that the latter is in its greatest splendor. I left these things alone; the eye cannot grasp everything.

In the afternoon I returned to the Esterházy Collection again and then went to the Italian Theatre. There Rossini’s opera *Corradino* was performed. Mrs. Dardanelli and David sang. I find this prejudice unworthy of our own musical culture. The music is not a mere collection of notes; it is a living spirit that requires the voice to breathe. I find myself wishing to hear the piece once more, for it is in the repetition that the true nature of the art reveals itself. The tension between the individual voice and the universal chorus is a theme we know well, and here it is realized with a freshness that I cannot help but admire.

I hope you are well and that the boys are behaving themselves. The journey continues, and the mind finds new material for reflection in every landscape.

Your affectionate husband,

Dear Marie,

I am writing to you by the light of the full moon and a thin candle. We have arrived in Duxan, which is located approximately in the middle of the road from Prague to Töplitz. As I only learned where we were a half hour before writing, I could not inform you beforehand.

The journey through Bohemia was in the most beautiful and loveliest sunshine one can imagine. The country is indeed wonderful, but the villages are miserable. I will reach Töplitz tomorrow at noon and Dresden in the evening, perhaps not until Sunday.

In Tiek I met Prof. Hinrichs, who is moving to Halle. Also Mr. Friedrich von Schlegel was there; his name was only mentioned to me after he had driven off. I was glad to see him again, even if it was only briefly.

The mood here is calm. I think of you and the children in Berlin. The landscape is so bright and clear that one almost forgets how far one is from home. I hope that the post will soon bring us together again.

Your faithful husband

Hegel

P.S. Dresden, 11 Oct. 24.

My dear Marie,

I am sitting in Duxan, a little more than halfway on the road from Prague to Töplitz. I departed Prague after 11 o'clock and have been driving all day through Bohemia in the most beautiful, loveliest sunshine. The country is beautiful, but the villages are wretched, which constantly holds one back and clouds the view. I only learned half an hour before writing where I actually am, which shows the uncertainty of the postal routes here. Tomorrow at noon I will arrive in Töplitz and be in Dresden in the evening; perhaps not until Sunday.

I am writing by the light of the full moon and a thin candle, which gives me a peculiar stillness. I miss you and the boys very much, but the journey demands its toll. I will try to sleep well in order to have fresh strength tomorrow. Kiss the children from me warmly and do not be angry with me that I am so far from you.

Your
Hegel

P.S. In Töplitz I met Prof. Hinrichs, who is moving to Halle, and Mr. Friedrich von Schlegel, whose name was only mentioned to me after his departure.

Vienna, September 21, 1824

My dear Marie,

I am sitting down to tell you about my stay in Vienna today, after I have returned home from the opera. The day was full of impressions, both in spirit and in body, and I hope you will forgive the brevity, as fatigue is now overcoming me.

In the morning, I began with a visit to St. Stephen's Church, where I took a brief overview of the imperial picture painting in the Belvedere. The works of art speak of a certain perfection that unfolds only in the history of freedom, but today I limit myself to mere perception. Afterwards, I hurried to the post office to receive your letter – a precious comfort in the distance – and subsequently I had to settle my passport matters at the customs office, a tedious but necessary duty of the traveler.

In the evening, however, the true pleasure awaited: the Italian Opera. Rubini and Donzelli appeared as tenors and sang a duet that deeply impressed me. The bassist Lablache was also present, although he did not have a leading role. It is interesting to see how German vocal art shows itself here; the singer Eckerlin is currently present, and he is compared with Madame Milder. Madame Fodor is playing in Othello today, which indicates a significant performance. After the opera, there followed a pas de deux by two Frenchmen, which reflected the elegance of the Parisian school.

On the way home, I found Lilli and Klein at my house. They are staying here this week and have spent the last three evenings at the Casperl and German Theatre, without seeing or hearing the Italian Opera. We have agreed to go out together, for their presence enlivens the household. Partheys young wife was unwell in her room, which explains her absence.

I will remain in Vienna as long as the money for the opera and the return journey lasts. It is a precious time that I am using to experience the culture of this metropolis, before I return to the duty of my lectures. I am now going to dinner to still the fatigue.

Your faithful
G. W. F. Hegel

Vienna, September 25.

My dear!

I am writing to you from Vienna, where I shall remain as long as my purse allows and the Italian opera justifies my stay. It is a city that must not be measured by the intellect, but by the sense for the beautiful and the great.

In the morning I was in St. Stephen's Church and then visited the Belvedere. I had only a brief overview of the imperial painting collection; one cannot view everything there, but the impression is tremendous. Afterwards I settled my papers at the customs office and collected my letters. Now that the errands are done, I am waiting for the evening.

The Italian opera is the pride of this city. Today the tenors Rubini and Donzelli sang; their duets were a feast for the ear. The bassist Lablache was also there, although he did not have a leading role. There is also a German singer here, Eckerlin; he is compared to Milder, which is a great compliment for him. Fodor will perform in Othello today. After the opera there was also a pas de deux by two Frenchmen from Paris, which crowned the evening.

At home I found Lilli and Klein. They have stayed this week and spent the last three evenings at the Casperl and the German Theatre. They have not yet seen or heard the Italian opera, but we have agreed to go out together in the future. Partheys young wife remained unwell in her room today.

I am now going to eat, as I have become hungry from walking and seeing. The evenings here are lively, and it is good to be among people who fill their time with art. I think of you and the children in Berlin and hope that you are well.

Your G. W. F. Hegel

Vienna, September 21.

My dear,

Vienna, October 4, 1824

My dear Marie,

I am writing to you from here, where the days are marked by the inspection of treasures. You know how much I value art and history, and so I had to devote myself today once again to Schönbrunn Palace and its views, in order to complete the image of Vienna in my mind. It is a laborious but rewarding task to open one’s eyes to beauty while the city rests in the evening light.

I must make a small remark to you, which you may find amusing. In Berlin, Potsdam, and Sanssouci, one paid a ducat each for admission to the various rooms. Even in Sanssouci, at the grave of Frederick the Great and his dogs, ducats and thalers are demanded. I advise you, my dears, to keep the ducats and thalers that would be due for admission in Berlin and instead use them for the travel costs to Vienna. The finest treasures to be seen here surpass in their reality what can currently be viewed in Berlin. It is therefore worth distributing the funds differently in order to experience the true greatness of art.

In the afternoon, I visited Schönbrunn and its views again. Afterwards, I went to the menagerie. One could only see the enclosure there, for most of the animals had already fallen asleep. I saw the elephant and the ostrich, which were still awake. I also looked at the plants, but I could not see the flowers, as they cannot be well recognized with a lantern. I have postponed it to another time.

Today there was neither Fodor, nor Dardanelli, nor Lablache to be heard. I saw only part of a piece at the Leopoldstheater. I am bringing you the ticket for this performance. Tomorrow I plan to take the gallop carriage early in the morning in order to continue my journey.

Please read part of this letter to my friend, Privy Councillor Schulze. He will surely take pleasure in it.

I kiss you and the children warmly.

Your faithful
Hegel

Vienna, October 4, 1824.

Dearest Marie,

But even in Sanssouci itself, ducats and thalers are demanded for everything, even for the grave of Frederick the Great and his dogs. I advise you to keep together the ducats and thalers needed for Berlin and use them for the travel expenses to Vienna, for the finest treasures in Vienna are in reality greater than what one can currently see in Berlin.

This afternoon I was again in Schönbrunn and enjoyed the views. Then I visited the menagerie. I saw only the plan of the establishment. I saw the elephant and the ostrich, but the other animals had already fallen asleep. With the plants, I could not see the flowers, as one cannot recognize them with a lantern; I have postponed it to another time.

Today there was no Fodor, no Dardanelli, and no Lablache. I saw only part of a piece at the Leopoldstheater and am bringing the ticket with me. Tomorrow morning I take the gallop carriage.

Please read the part of this letter that refers to our joint plans to my friend, Privy Councillor Schulze. He will surely be interested in it.

The days here pass quickly, and I often think of you and the children in Berlin. The air is different here, and the way of life too. I hope you and the boys are well.

Your faithful
G. W. F. Hegel

Vienna, October 4th, Evening

My dear Marie,

It has become late, and I wish to give you a brief report on what the day itself held. I drove to Schönbrunn again today to enjoy the views, which I have already described to you before; they are always refreshing. Afterwards, I visited the menagerie. One could only see the plan of it, for most of the animals had already fallen asleep. I saw the elephant and the ostrich, but of the other creatures there was nothing to be seen. I also saw the plants, but we could not see the flowers themselves, as one cannot recognize much in the dark with a lantern; I have postponed this to another day.

As for the costs, the matter is arranged in these gardens and palaces as follows: For the entrance to the various rooms in Berlin, Potsdam, and Sanssouci, one pays a ducat. In Sanssouci itself, they demand ducats and thalers for everything, even for the entrance to the tomb of Frederick the Great and his dogs. It is a peculiar arrangement, but one must accustom oneself to it. I advise my acquaintances who wish to visit these places to collect the necessary ducats and thalers for the entrance and better use them for the travel costs to Vienna, for the finest treasures here are in reality greater than everything one can currently see in Berlin.

In the evening, I went to the Leopoldstheater and saw part of a play. I am bringing the ticket with me. Today there was neither Fodor, nor Dardanelli, nor Lablache; that is a disappointment one can hardly grasp. Tomorrow morning I intend to take the gallop wagon to continue my journey.

Please, read the first part of this letter to my friend, the Privy Councillor Schulze, when you see him; he will be pleased that I am again in Vienna and admiring the treasures.

I am healthy and vigorous, though tired from walking. Think of me in your kindness.

Your faithful G. W. F. Hegel

Töplitz, September 11, 1824.

My dear Marie,

The day here in the spa town has a certain heaviness that reminds me of the inevitable in world history, but I set aside the great concepts and simply write to you how I have been getting along. On Thursday afternoon I visited the Gallery in Dresden. It is always good to contemplate art, which shapes the spirit, even if it is only a forerunner of inner freedom. Afterwards we took a walk to the Linksche Bath. The evening belonged to Tiek and the Countess von Finkenstein, who performed a comedy by Hollberg. It was most entertaining and truly brilliant; I left the performance before it was over, for my watch already showed 1 o'clock in the morning.

The noise of nature woke me shortly thereafter: a thunderstorm with moonlight. A watchman nearby confirmed the hour to me. I undressed and fell asleep again. At ½5 o'clock I had to be ready, but the departure was delayed. The weather was unpleasant, so that I had to put on a coat, an overcoat, and a cloak instead of my silk dressing gown. We drove in a shared carriage with a mixed company: an actress with child and dog, as well as three Württembergers.

Mrs. Stock called out to us the view from the Nollendorfer height. The view down the road to Bohemia was rich and beautiful. We passed the Austrian border and the customs station at Peterswalde, still before Nollendorf. Without complaint and without long delay we were through. It is lacking that you are not here. Please give my regards to Mrs. Stock.

Your G. W. F. Hegel

Töplitz, September 11, 1824.

My dear Marie!

It is now 1 o'clock at night. A clap of thunder and the moonlight woke me before I could get dressed again. I was ready by 1 o'clock, but the departure was delayed; the unpleasant weather forced me to put on a dress, an overcoat, and a cloak instead of the silk nightgown. Hegel

My dear Marie,

It is Friday, October 1st, and I am writing to you from a journey that broadens the eyes, even though the mind longs for the quiet of our Berlin rooms. Today I visited the Prater, a stretch of woodland with green grass, where the trees are trimmed as if in a strictly maintained garden. One walks there between the trunks, not under leaves, and the sky, which was beautifully blue today, is clearly visible. The sun is now lower, and the shadows cast by the hedges cut into vertical, flat walls give the place a special, almost artificial order. The landscape is in the most beautiful light, and at the end of the garden one sees the richest earth, bounded by the hills Leopoldiberg and Kahlenberg, which are about an hour away.

In the Prater itself there are countless taverns, bowling alleys, merry-go-rounds, and optical cabinets that offer "optical room travels." Particularly striking were several very elegant coffee pavilions; here the word "Kaffeh" is spelled correctly, which I noticed as a small satisfaction. After long walking and out of pure fatigue, I finally sought rest in the Leopoldstadt Theatre. Schuster played the role of a Magister excellently and spoke high German in doing so. The second performance was the *Zauberbirn*, a piece I hardly wish to mention, except that I saw it.

I returned home in the most beautiful moonlight. The fine weather remains uncorruptibly faithful. I went to dinner and have confessed that I envy such points, this light cheerfulness, and the clear light a little. I think of you and the children and wish that you are doing well there.

Your
G. W. F. Hegel

My dear Marie,

I am sitting in the hotel this evening and writing to you, while the lovely weather, which has accompanied us so faithfully, is also showing itself outside. I was in the Prater today. The garden is laid out here as in Schönbrunn, with broad, large avenues. But what particularly struck me: the trees and shrubs are not left in their natural state, but are cut into vertical, flat walls. Some trees are shaped like fans or like pears, which have been cut into a flat circle on their trunk. One walks between the trees, not under leaves, and the sky is freely visible above. Today it was beautifully blue, and since the sun stands lower, the cut walls cast long shadows.

At the end of the garden, the view opens onto the richest countryside, where Leopoldiberg and Kahlenberg, about an hour away, form the boundary. The light lay on the landscape today in the most beautiful way. The Prater itself is a forest with green grass, but entirely without undergrowth or bushes between the trunks. There is an innumerable number of taverns, bowling alleys, merry-go-rounds, and optical rooms. I found some very elegant coffee pavilions; it is noteworthy that here the word “Kaffeh” is spelled correctly.

After long wandering about, I went to the Leopoldstadt Theatre for rest out of fatigue. Schuster played the role of a Magister excellently and spoke High German. The second performance was The Magic Pear. Then I went home in the most beautiful moonlight. Then it was time for soup. I envy such places for their quiet. Kiss the dear boys from me.

Your
G. W. F. Hegel

My dear Marie,

Today I spent the day in the Prater. It is a large forest with green grass, between the tree trunks without any undergrowth. One strolls through this magnificent, open space, and the weather has remained faithful and beautiful, as I like it.

The trees are like fans or like a pear that has been cut into a disc on its trunk. One walks between the trees, not under leaves, so that the magnificently blue sky remains freely visible above us. I am envious of such spots that so refresh the soul. It is strange how much one longs here for the quiet one has in Berlin. I sat in the coffee house – the word is here, as they say, correctly spelled – and enjoyed the elegant atmosphere of the pavilions.

Farewell, my dears.

Your faithful Hg.

My dear Marie,

It is Monday morning, September 27, and I am writing to you from Vienna. Yesterday, after going to the Prater, I went to the Leopoldstadt Theatre. There, an introduction was performed in which Schuster appeared. He played an older merchant with a young lady, which was quite amusing. In addition, *The Magic Orange* was performed once more. It was the second time I had seen it.

Unfortunately, the weather has changed. It has been raining continuously since Sunday, and this morning it is still wet. Therefore, on Sunday morning, I stayed at home because of the heavy rain. However, after lunch, I had myself driven to the Augarten and to Nußdorf, despite the bad weather. On the way, I saw a pear tree that was as large as a pear tree can be. It was full of blossoms and had already borne fruit. I picked a blossom and am enclosing it with this letter. One blossom is for you, the other for the one who has blossomed from this land.

I now have a provisional impression of what the Augarten and Nußdorf are like. I wish the young people had been with me. You would certainly not have been too old to be amused a second time. The heat and the dampness are hard on me, but the prospect of seeing you again soon makes the hardships of the journey bearable. I greet Karl and Immanuel warmly and kiss you.

Your
G.W.F. Hegel

Vienna, September 27.

My dear Marie,

Today, after visiting the Prater, I went to the Leopoldstadt Theatre. The play "The Magic Pear" was performed again; I saw it for the second time. In the prologue, Schuster appeared, in the manner of an older merchant with a young woman. It is a pleasant picture that presents itself to the spectator.

But the sky was not favorable. It rained all Sunday and this morning still in torrents, so that I had to rest in the morning. Only after lunch did I have myself driven, despite the weather, to the Augarten and to Nußdorf. I have only taken a preliminary look at the places, yet the impression of the lush vegetation has remained strong. On the way, a pear tree caught my eye, of a size that a pear tree can only be. It was still covered with blossom and had already borne fruit.

I close this letter with two blossoms. One is for you, the other for the one who has blossomed forth from this land. I wish the young ones had been with me; you yourself would, I think, not have been too old to enjoy it a second time.

Your faithful H.

My dear Marie,

My body still feels the strain of yesterday's march in my bones, but my mind is lively. This morning I held the writing lesson with you without first going home to apologize; it was a pleasure to see you again. Afterwards, I stood in the Lichtenstein picture gallery until noon. I maintain that I could not exhaust the treasures of this museum even after ten more visits. The gallery is almost half an hour away from Währing, where I went after the midday hour. There I visited Professor Rembold, my countryman, who is younger than I and whose knowledge of my writings is not unknown.

Subsequently, I crossed an arm of the Danube to dine in the Augarten. I ate in my lodging, where the fateful card game takes place, and had a good appetite. The food in the Augarten was more delicious and cheaper to me than ever before. After the meal, I strolled around in the garden. I notice that the people here stay home too much; traveling and a change of environment does not come as easily to them as it does to us. I wish you and the children all the best.

Your
G. W. F. Hegel
